extracted.intended_audience: mathematics teachers, mathematics educators, and advanced students of mathematics interested in pedagogy
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and standards for teaching and presenting pure mathematics so as to cultivate appreciation of beauty, rigorous reasoning, and unity of subject matter. Covers methods for arithmetic, geometry, algebra, calculus/infinity, proofs, textbooks and the role of symbolic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question the purpose and ideal of the study
rubrics_metrics.description: In regard to every form of human activity it is necessary that the question should be asked from time to time, What is its purpose and ideal? In what way does it contribute to the beauty of human existence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or design a course/activity by articulating its ultimate aim (beauty, permanent possessions of the world) rather than only practical mechanisms. Avoid letting mechanical or remote utility claims substitute for a clear ideal; keep alive a prefiguring vision of the 'temple' the studies should lead to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mathematics as an end in itself (not merely technical training)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty... What is best in mathematics deserves not merely to be learnt as a task, but to be assimilated as a part of daily thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula and instruction should emphasize pure mathematics' aesthetic and intellectual value, not only its application to machines or practical tasks. Foster assimilation and repeated contemplation of mathematical ideas rather than rote utility-driven learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awaken belief in reason and the value of demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the chief ends served by mathematics, when rightly taught, is to awaken the learner's belief in reason, his confidence in the truth of what has been demonstrated, and in the value of demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should build trust in proof and demonstration by showing reasons for rules and the reliability of deductive methods. Avoid methods that present rules as arbitrary 'will of the teacher' and instead give grounds appealing to the learner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedagogical mystification and rote rule-teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: At present ... the boy or girl is given a set of rules, which present themselves as neither true nor false, but as merely the will of the teacher... the reasons of rules should be set forth by whatever means most readily appeal to the childish mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace blind rule-following with explanations and demonstrations suited to children's understanding. Do not persist in teaching known fallacies or unquestioned tricks; do not leave algebra/applied rules as mystifying prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry instruction: begin with obvious truths and concrete drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: In geometry, instead of the tedious apparatus of fallacious proofs for obvious truisms which constitutes the beginning of Euclid, the learner should be allowed at first to assume the truth of everything obvious, and should be instructed in the demonstrations of theorems which are at once startling and easily verifiable by actual drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use startling, easily verifiable theorems and encourage drawing the figure in many shapes so abstract relations emerge. Give proofs after familiarity; exclude definitely fallacious methods (e.g., superposition) from the start, and when strict proof is hard, render results acceptable via contrasted arguments and illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra instruction: explain the shift from arithmetic to generality
rubrics_metrics.description: In algebra the mind is first taught to consider general truths... the use of letters is a mystery... the teacher should explain the chasm which divides it from arithmetic, and assist the learner in his groping efforts at comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify that letters represent generality not hidden particular numbers; show the purpose of abstraction. Avoid carrying forward arithmetic's rote-rule style into algebra; help learners understand why algebraic methods work and what generality means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the modern theory of the infinite early and clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution of the difficulties which formerly surrounded the mathematical infinite ... Georg Cantor has found the answer ... This stupendous fact ought to produce a revolution in the higher teaching of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present Cantor/Dedekind's resolutions of infinite-paradoxes to remove confusion and to enable logical precision in higher mathematics. Use the new doctrine to sweep away compromises that encouraged accepting fallacious but 'practical' arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve purity and strictness of reasoning; lead backward to foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: If we are considering mathematics as an end in itself ... it is very desirable to preserve the purity and strictness of its reasoning. Accordingly those who have attained a sufficient familiarity with its easier portions should be led backward from propositions to more fundamental principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After initial agreement with plausible propositions, guide learners to examine foundations and derive earlier premises from central principles. Encourage sceptical inquiry into first principles and study elementary portions afresh in terms of underlying logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize unity and systematic development in presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the great majority of mathematical text-books there is a total lack of unity in method and of systematic development of a central theme... In the greatest works, unity and inevitability are felt as in the unfolding of a drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks and courses should present subjects as logical wholes with a central theme; avoid disparate propositions proved by ad hoc methods or space devoted to curiosities. Encourage dwelling on central principles and the structural connections among topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proofs beautiful and each step intrinsically valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic excellence of mathematics is only to be found where the reasoning is rigidly logical: ... a chain of argument in which every link is important on its own account, in which there is an air of ease and lucidity throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor proofs and demonstrations where each step is meaningful and contributes aesthetically, not solely instrumental to the conclusion. Seek generalizations that make intermediate steps significant. Avoid arguments that use more premises than necessary; elegance arises from employing only essential principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer essential axioms to avoid diminishing generality
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a merit in Euclid that he advances as far as he is able to go without employing the axiom of parallels... every new axiom diminishes the generality of the resulting theorems, and the greatest possible generality is before all things to be sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving results, isolate and use only those assumptions required; avoid introducing unnecessary axioms. Evaluate arguments by their generality and minimal dependence on extra premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete illustrations and varied figures before formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Where theorems are difficult, they should be first taught as exercises in geometrical drawing, until the figure has become thoroughly familiar; it will then be an agreeable advance to be taught the logical connections...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach difficult theorems via drawing and multiple concrete instances so the abstract relation emerges; only then proceed to formal proofs. Encourage drawing the illustrating figure 'in all possible cases and shapes' to reveal invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantic fullness in early proofs; contrast informal arguments with demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: In this early stage proofs should not be given with pedantic fullness; definitely fallacious methods ... should be rigidly excluded from the first, but where, without such methods, the proof would be very difficult, the result should be rendered acceptable by arguments and illustrations which are explicitly contrasted with demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In beginners' instruction, give intuitive or illustrative arguments rather than full formal proof; make clear the distinction between acceptable informal arguments and genuine demonstrations, and postpone full rigor until readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter the 'practical spirit' that overemphasizes results over method
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain practical spirit, a desire for rapid progress, for conquest of new realms, is responsible for the undue emphasis upon results which prevails in mathematical instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist prioritizing speed and new results at the cost of depth and method. Design instruction so the process, structure, and understanding of proofs is valued as much as the final theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce symbolic logic as the unifying foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the separate studies ... have each been viewed as a logical whole, the learner will be able to understand the fundamental science which unifies and systematises the whole of deductive reasoning. This is symbolic logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach symbolic logic (analysis of actual examples of deductive reasoning) to reveal a small number of fundamental principles that underlie all pure mathematics. Use logic to show the unity and inevitability of mathematical deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present mathematics as independent and dealing with absolute necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics takes us still further from what is human, into the region of absolute necessity, to which not only the actual world, but every possible world, must conform...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame mathematics as addressing ideal, non-human necessities rather than merely laws of human thought; this perspective strengthens appreciation of mathematical beauty and objective truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate austerer virtues and the love of truth through instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: For the health of the moral life, for ennobling the tone of an age or a nation, the austerer virtues have a strange power ... Of these austerer virtues the love of truth is the chief, and in mathematics, more than elsewhere, the love of truth may find encouragement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pedagogy to foster habits of mind—candour, fidelity to evidence, love of truth—rather than merely technical ability. Use mathematics to encourage lofty intellectual character and the habit of disciplined thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let utility be the sole guide for selecting mathematical studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility, therefore, can be only a consolation in moments of discouragement, not a guide in directing our studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing topics and structuring curricula, do not base choices solely on foreseeable practical applications; value abstract work for its potential long-term transformative effects and unpredictable future usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analysis of real deductive examples to teach the rules of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The true method of discovery in symbolic logic, and probably also the best method for introducing the study to a learner ... is the analysis of actual examples of deductive reasoning, with a view to the discovery of the principles employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach inference rules by dissecting genuine arguments; extract the few fundamental principles embedded in our ratiocinative instincts rather than presenting abstract rules in isolation.
